I probably wouldn't go lower than C++11, unless you are in a situation where you know you will have to use an earlier version. TBH, you probably wouldn't do too much damage by going earlier, but you might pick up some habits/practices that wouldn't be advisable in more modern versions of C++. A lot of the new features in C++11/14 are really convenient, make life easier, and help to make more stable programs. Personally, I've began to really love C++11.

It doesn't matter really. Newer versions of the C++ standard have incorporated some "impure" features. But that's only important if you think that's important.

If you are just starting out, you shouldn't be worried about writing efficient code. You should be worried about making SOMETHING work. But be warned. Later standards have features which encourage "Bad Practices". Once you start learning Data Structures and Algorithms, then, you will need to take the time to figure out what features are considered "Bad Practice".

Until then, just use whatever.

It depends what you are trying to accomplish.

If you really want to be a guru expert and have tons of time, then it's best to work your way forward through the releases. That way you will understand older code, and you'll understand why the newer methods are better or worse in different cases. I started last year at the beginning with K&R ( regular c ) because my office had a ton of old school guys. I quickly learned that to get a good base, then once I got around to learning the C++ 11 features I really had an excellent grasp on what the new features were doing behind the scenes. Then I started bitching about everyone in the office being archaic :) Since I really needed a deep understanding, I took the long route.

These days in engineering schools, they teach you C++11 first just because it gives them the ability to glaze over the grainy details and stick to the logic and algorithms. If I was picking a starting point, and didn't have a need to understand outdated code, then I would definitely go with C++11. Most of the latest compilers will support at least 11, but some may not have every feature of 14 yet, so just check your compiler support.
